summary:
We will build a browser game for NASA Space Apps. 

Kids run a Moon outpost for 10 days. Each day they get 5 power blocks. They spend the blocks on Air, Shield and Food. 

A real NASA solar storm is coming, and the kids must get ready for it.
At the end, the game explains in plain words why the crew was safe or not.
details:
What it does and how it works

SOL SHIELD is a browser game for kids aged 7 to 12. The player runs a small Moon outpost for 10 days. A day on another world is called a sol. Each sol the player gets 5 power blocks. The player spends the blocks on three things : Air, Shield and Food. A block spent on one thing is a block the others do not get, so no choice is free.

Each mission uses a real solar storm from NASA's DONKI database. First the player sees a sunspot watch. Then a flare warning. Then the storm hits. If the player built the Shield early, the crew stays healthy. If not, the crew gets a high radiation dose. The player can also ask Mission Control on Earth for advice. This costs one power block and the answer comes after a delay.

When the mission ends, the game never shows "game over". It shows a Why Chain instead. The Why Chain explains in plain words what caused the result. It also shows the real NASA flare date and class. Then the player can try again with a different real storm.


Benefits and intended impact

Kids learn that astronauts must plan for space weather before it arrives. They also learn that power, air, food and shielding compete for the same limited supply. We want kids to leave the game understanding one real rule of deep space survival. Teachers and parents can use it with no download and no login.

Tools used

We used HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Vite. We used NASA's DONKI data through the NASA Open APIs. We used Vercel to host the game for free.

What makes it creative

Every kid plays a real storm from NASA's archive, not an invented one. The Mission Control delay shows that crews far from Earth must decide for themselves. The Why Chain turns a loss into a lesson. Each replay uses a different storm and a different arrival day, so kids try new plans.

What we considered

We kept the game to three resources so young players are not overwhelmed. We wrote the text in short, simple sentences and explained each science word. We made the game safe for kids: no accounts, no emails and no personal data.
